title: English language education in the multilingual Global South
abstract: Abstract Throughout the Global South, English functions as just one component of a broader linguistic landscape. Consequently, integrating it into curricula or instructional medium necessitates valuing the rich linguistic capital of educational stakeholders. This Special Issue offers a critical re-examination of English language education (ELE) across the multilingual Global South. Moving beyond rigid, Anglo-centric monolingual mandates, the collection captures the ‘multilingual turn’ by addressing the persistent gap between macro-level policies and micro-level classroom realities. The issue progresses across three key themes: socio-affective and trauma-informed decolonial frameworks; teacher agency, leadership and professional development; and classroom practices on GenAI technologies and translanguaging. Across geographical contexts including Sri Lanka, Morocco, Vietnam, India, South Africa, Pakistan, and Iran, the studies demonstrate that leveraging learners’ home languages scaffolds conceptual understanding, alleviates anxiety, and fosters inclusive learning. The special issue posits multilingualism as a vital instrument of epistemic justice and educational equity in Global Sou

title: When Pashtu keeps English learning alive in Pakistan: a case study
abstract: Abstract This study explores stakeholder perspectives and teachers’ practices in multilingual primary classrooms in two public-sector schools in the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province of Pakistan. Given the impact of classroom language on student learning and engagement, the study examines the views of frontline educators and communities in relation to languages used in classrooms. Using the school as a hub, data were collected through semi-structured interviews with teachers, teacher leaders, and parents, as well as focus group discussions with community members. Classroom observations identified selected teachers’ language-use practices. The findings reveal that stakeholders recognize the importance of the mother tongue and/or learners’ own languages for identity and belonging, yet acknowledge linguistic hierarchies, with Urdu as the lingua franca and English as a language of opportunity. Teachers regularly use learners’ mother tongue and translanguaging to aid comprehension and conceptual understanding. A policy–practice gap is evident, highlighting the need for alignment to address classroom realities and learner needs and bring in targeted teacher training.

title: Teaching interactional competence via ‘worked examples’
abstract: Abstract This action research study reports on two iterations of a course designed to develop students’ Interactional Competence (IC) in assessed group discussions at a UK higher education institution. Addressing the limitations of traditional ‘useful phrases’ approaches to teaching speaking, the course adapted Lam’s (2025) ‘worked examples’ framework by integrating simplified conversation-analytic transcripts, guided noticing questions, explicit links to assessment criteria, and practice test tasks. Data from learners’ written reflections and post-session interviews indicated that students developed a more sophisticated understanding of interaction as a jointly organised and relational process. They demonstrated heightened awareness of turn-taking, co-construction, listenership, pragmatic variation, and task management. The study suggests that transcript-based noticing tasks provide a practical model for integrating interactional competence into classroom speaking instruction and assessment design.

title: What do EFL teachers know about dyslexia? Evidence from Türkiye
abstract: Abstract Dyslexia poses challenges in EFL learning, yet many teachers are expected to support learners with dyslexia despite having limited training or guidance. This study explores Turkish primary school EFL teachers’ knowledge of dyslexia, areas of uncertainty, and perceived support needs. Survey data from 288 teachers and interviews with 47 teachers show that awareness is shaped mainly by uncertainty rather than firmly held misconceptions. While most teachers identify dyslexia as a literacy-related difficulty, simplified views such as ‘letter reversal’ remain common, particularly among those without formal training. More experienced teachers reported higher awareness, suggesting that knowledge is often gained through classroom experience rather than systematic preparation. Teachers highlighted the absence of dyslexia-focused professional development and called for practical, English-specific training and stronger institutional support. The findings emphasize the need for practice-oriented teacher education to support inclusive EFL classrooms.

title: Pedagogical translanguaging in English language classes in India
abstract: Abstract In English classrooms in Global South contexts, such as India, teachers spontaneously draw on learners’ home language(s) to facilitate learning. This classroom-based study explores the scope of systematically integrating L1 in English classrooms through Pedagogic Translanguaging (PT). It reports the implementation of pedagogical translanguaging by a Grade 8 English teacher in her classrooms in India. By integrating Malayalam (L1) with English (L2) across six of her narrative reading lessons, the study demonstrates that teacher-led PT can scaffold reading comprehension and oral production by systematically drawing on learners’ multilingual resources. Qualitative analysis of classroom interactions reveals five micro-functions of PT to teach academic English, thereby reducing learning load and enhancing learner participation. Findings suggest that planned translanguaging offers an alternative to rigid English-only policies, promoting multilingual pedagogy, linguistic diversity, and social justice in Global South classrooms.

title: Enhancing English comprehension through translanguaging in South African township classrooms
abstract: Abstract This study looks at how teachers use translanguaging as a way to make learning fairer in South African township schools. In these schools, English is seen as the only proper language for teaching, which leaves multilingual learners at a disadvantage. Few studies have looked closely at how translanguaging works in real classroom moments as a fairness-focused approach, so this research fills that gap. It focuses on a Grade 8 classroom and examines how a teacher deliberately uses translanguaging to support learners’ understanding of English texts and to build shared knowledge through flexible language use. The research was done as a qualitative case study. The researcher observed lessons, recorded interactions, and interviewed the teacher. The findings show that when teachers deliberately use learners’ full language resources, they create spaces where all learners can participate more fully, leading to deeper understanding and more active involvement in lessons. The study argues that this fairness-focused approach should be included in teacher training and assessment systems as a way to decolonise education.

title: Translanguaging identities, ideologies, and pedagogy among ELT trainees in Spain
abstract: Abstract This article examines the linguistic identities, ideologies, and attitudes of pre-service ELT practitioners from an English as a Lingua Franca (ELF) perspective regarding translanguaging. We track students’ identity and attitudinal changes across the official 4-year BA in English Studies (ES) in two ELF settings: a Catalan bilingual and a Spanish monolingual university. Our mixed-methods approach includes the analysis of surveys (n = 319) and interviews (n = 12). The results suggest that 1st/2nd-year students show disengagement with translanguaging and hold monolingual attitudes toward languages whose mixing is inappropriate. 3rd/4th-year students seem to have gained some multilingual competence, displaying increased metalinguistic awareness of their linguistic repertoires, and welcoming some limited Pedagogical Translanguaging. This contributes to tracing the evolution of ideologies that range from NS-oriented beliefs to more ELF-aware attitudes, suggesting the need for a shift from prescriptivist approaches toward a critical focus on ELF Pedagogy (ELFP) in Higher Education and teacher training.

title: Generative AI in multilingual Global South classrooms
abstract: Abstract ELT is shifting towards multilingual approaches that value diverse linguistic practices. In the Global South, where diversity and colonial histories intersect, this shift raises concerns. The rise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted debate about whether these technologies can respond to multilingual realities. While GenAI is praised for personalising instruction and fostering engagement, language-of-instruction and design risks may re-establish linguistic hierarchy and marginalise community-based literacies. Drawing on collaborative autoethnographic data from four educators, this article explores teaching experiences and perceptions of opportunities and tensions in GenAI use in multilingual classrooms, particularly Vietnam and Iran. The conclusions suggest that educators perceived context-specific cultural and pedagogical tensions requiring critical adaptation to promote linguistic justice and inclusivity. Rather than making broad generalisations, the article offers an exploratory, educator-centred account of how GenAI may support and constrain multilingual resources, pedagogical judgment, multilingual meaning-making, and AI-mediated forms of ‘accept

title: Exploring Creativity through Writing: A Handbook for Teachers, Alan Maley and Sharoon Sunny
Key Concepts in ELT Equity
abstract: Abstract Equity as a value and principle dismantles discrimination and ensures justice for all educational stakeholders. Equity is one of the key terms in DEI (diversity, equity, and inclusion), a concept of social justice that has become a major institutional mission. Seeking equity in English language teaching (ELT) means establishing fairness in terms of diverse identities, including gender, race, class, ethnicity, language, sexuality, and disability. This short discussion on equity in ELT addresses the difference between equity and equality and two types of equity-based educational interventions: (1) representational intervention to amplify the representation of a marginalized group in teaching materials and pedagogies, and (2) accommodation intervention to remove institutional and societal inequalities by providing specific support to meet the unique needs of individuals or groups. Stakeholders should recognize that equitable outcomes cannot be achieved without ensuring adequate resources, rigorous curriculum, teacher training, and administrative support, which together enhance pedagogical quality.

title: Teaching interculturality through Southern multilingualisms: EFL teacher agency
abstract: Abstract EFL occupies a paradoxical space in Morocco, tasked with teaching interculturality within language hierarchies, marginalizing local cultures and knowledge systems. This research draws on in-depth interviews and classroom observations with seventeen Moroccan EFL teachers, aiming to investigate: (1) how teachers perceive the impact of multilingual hierarchies on teaching interculturality, and (2) how they leverage multilingual resources for intercultural pedagogy. Findings reveal that: first, teachers conceptualize linguistic power relations as persistent barriers to equitable intercultural education. The dominance of English and French often (re)produces the privileging of Western Anglophone cultural content while systemically marginalizing local Amazigh and Darija knowledge systems in EFL classrooms. Second, teachers employ nuanced strategies of adaptation and subversion to navigate the Eurocentric limitations of prescribed materials. Classroom observations identified certain practices that constitute what is termed ‘critical multilingual adaptation’, as teachers use the textbook as a scaffold while simultaneously destabilizing its cultural assumptions and referencing loca

title: Rethinking CELTA observations: using text-chat in Teaching Practice
abstract: Abstract Observation is central to initial teacher education courses like CELTA, yet the learning of observers often receives little attention. This article reports on a doctoral action research study across two part-time CELTA courses in the UK, exploring the use of synchronous text-chat during Teaching Practice to foster dialogic engagement and emergent noticing. Using cycles of planning, acting, observing, and reflecting, I investigated how tutor prompts in chat guided attention, how tensions arose between observers and those being observed, and how group dynamics influenced learning. Data from journals, focus groups, and interviews revealed that collaborative text-chat can promote reflective noticing and shift observation from performance evaluation toward shared professional development. The article concludes with practical recommendations for CELTA tutors and teacher educators seeking to make observation more participatory and developmental.

title: Reforming the foreign language classroom: Empowering learners to take ownership Katja Heim, Leni Dam, Annika Albrecht and Carmen Becker (eds.)
Principles and strategies of multilingual pedagogy: insights from India
abstract: Abstract In multilingual societies, effective language education requires pedagogies that draw on learners’ full linguistic repertoires. Research on multilingual pedagogy such as translanguaging highlight the value of integrating students’ home languages to support meaning-making, participation and inclusion. This article reports on a project introducing multilingual pedagogy in English classrooms within English-medium government schools in Karnataka, India. Data were collected from 74 teachers through questionnaires, focus group discussions and interviews following a 6-day professional development programme. Findings indicate that teachers most frequently adopted principles of learner comfort, confidence and inclusivity in implementing strategies such as using home languages systematically, encouraging multilingual responses and building peer support. Teachers reported increased classroom participation, reduced anxiety about English and greater engagement in activities. However, challenges related to lesson planning, time management and assessment remained. The study offers insights into how to implement multilingual pedagogy in English-medium primary classrooms.

title: Using cinema to enhance high school students’ expression of appraisal
abstract: Abstract Given the essential role of appraisal in students’ successful social and literacy development, this study aimed to explore the impact of a cinema-based teaching unit on the capacity of EFL high school students with developing proficiency to express appraisal, specifically affect and judgment. Data were collected through pre- and post-tests in which students were asked to use adjectives to conceptualize the emotional and behavioral states portrayed in three clips from the film Brave. Results indicate that, following instruction, students significantly improved their production of affect and judgment. The study also provides a pedagogical framework to guide EFL practitioners in using films to teach appraisal.

title: Broadening the Horizon of TBLT: Plenary Addresses from the Second Decade of the International Conference on Task-Based Language Teaching, Martin East (ed.)
A response to ‘ELT teachers’ agency for wellbeing’
abstract: Abstract Sulis et al. (Sulis, G., A. Mairitsch, S. Babic, S. Mercer, and P. Resnik. 2024. ‘ELT Teachers’ Agency for Wellbeing.’ ELT Journal 78(2):198–206.) make some interesting and valid points about teacher agency, burnout and attrition. But, while fully accepting the value of what they have to say, in this response to their article I would like to suggest that it is not enough, and I attempt to suggest positive courses of action to deal with this long-running and ongoing threat to teacher wellbeing.

title: Cultural levels and orientations in business English materials
abstract: Abstract Internationally operating professionals communicate using English as a business lingua franca (BELF) with partners from various linguacultural backgrounds. A pedagogical challenge is addressing these complex transcultural interactions in a structured way that is not simplistic or stereotypical. To address this challenge, the concept of linguacultural levels and orientations is useful. In business, multiple levels of linguaculture interact: regional, organisational, work team, and individual. Simultaneously, three main linguacultural orientations operate: home, target, and universal. Employing a content analysis of five popular, globally distributed business English textbooks, this case study found that the textbooks emphasised regional and organisational levels of culture while deemphasising the team and individual levels. They contained a balance of orientations. Using textbooks as an example, the findings offer insights into how BE materials, including professionally written, authentic, learner-generated, or GenAI-created, can address culture in nuanced, structured, and balanced ways to prepare learners for transcultural workplace communication.

title: Integrating social justice language education into ELT
abstract: Abstract Social Justice Language Education (SJLE) belongs to a tradition of critical pedagogy stretching back over several decades based on the work of Paolo Freire, which gives it a number of important concepts, including conscientização. Critical pedagogy and social justice are ideas that have attracted significant interest in Applied Linguistics over recent years without resulting in widespread adoption of these ideas in ELT. Brown’s article proposes a solution to this issue incorporating strong Communicative Language Teaching approaches. In this counterpoint article, we critique the proposal, pointing out some fundamental issues that we think SJLE needs to address. We conclude by drawing attention to an extant proposal that is less radical and seems more realistic.

title: Revisiting social justice language education: some reflections
abstract: Abstract These reflections on the Point and Counterpoint by Brown (this issue) and Vincent and Ajayi (this issue) draw together and comment on shared themes and continuing issues.

title: Social justice language education through communicative language teaching
abstract: Abstract Despite increasing calls in academic literature for a more social justice-oriented approach to ELT, there remains some scepticism within our profession about how to implement it. This article problematises dominant practices in ELT today, identifying methodological, content-related, and ideological shortcomings that imply a need for significant change. Analysis of literature reveals that prescriptive models, common in many ELT contexts, do not adhere to some core principles of Communicative Language Teaching (CLT), and are out of step with academic discourse. Prescriptive ELT also fails to meet the profession’s obligations to effectively develop critical literacy. A re-examination of the core principles of CLT and associated methodologies reveals that ‘strong’ versions of CLT, which value learner input, negotiation of content and the incorporation of learners’ lived experiences, can easily be applied within a social justice-oriented curriculum, thereby addressing both ideological and methodological deficits.

title: From classroom to community: experiential learning in TESOL
abstract: Abstract This article examines a graduate-level TESOL initiative designed to bridge the gap between theoretical coursework and classroom practice through community-engaged experiential learning. Implemented in collaboration with federally funded Language Instruction for Newcomers to Canada (LINC) programs, the project paired 90 TESOL students with 18 adult ESL instructors. Over a structured, seven-phase process, students designed communicative listening and speaking activities aligned with the Canadian Language Benchmarks. Instructor feedback highlighted three key outcomes: students developed greater awareness of learner realities, demonstrated enhanced pedagogical competence, and experienced identity growth as legitimate educators. Notably, the initiative fostered reciprocal professional learning, with experienced teachers reporting renewed insight from student collaboration. Challenges included scheduling constraints, limited classroom observation opportunities, and delays in material delivery. Overall, this project affirms the potential of structured, community-based experiential learning to cultivate reflective, justice-oriented practitioners and offers a scalable model for TES

title: Adapting TBLT in Chinese secondary schools
abstract: Abstract While task-based language teaching (TBLT) has been extensively researched in controlled experimental settings at tertiary level, few studies have explored its adaptation to exam-oriented contexts, especially in secondary school education. To address this gap, this qualitative study explores how eight secondary school EFL teachers adapted TBLT to the demands of a Chinese exam-oriented education system. Through interviews and classroom observations, we uncover these teachers’ strategic adaptations and practices such as aligning tasks with exam content, strategically reducing task interaction time, and integrating elements of traditional teaching methods. These localized approaches reflect a pragmatic response to exam pressures while striving to maintain a focus on students’ communicative ability. Significantly, this study moves beyond simply documenting adaptations and the factors behind them to propose a novel Localized TBLT Framework. This framework offers practical steps for implementing TBLT in exam-oriented contexts, providing valuable guidance for EFL educators in similar settings globally.

title: Teacher activity groups to promote multilingual pedagogies in Vietnam
abstract: Abstract This article reports on a British Council—funded project that sought to develop teachers’ understandings of multilingual pedagogies in linguistically diverse primary schools in northern Vietnam. The project trained English teachers to lead teacher activity groups (TAGs) with colleagues from other subjects, based on the assumption that English teachers, due to their specialist knowledge of how languages are learned and taught, could act as agents of multilingualism in their schools. The study examined how TAGs supported teacher learning, collaboration, and the development of teacher leadership in multilingual pedagogy. Fifteen English teachers and thirty subject teachers participated across fifteen primary schools. Data included interviews, TAG meeting recordings, and reflective journals, analysed thematically. Findings indicate that TAGs fostered collaboration and increased awareness of multilingualism, although leadership development was uneven. The project identified some systemic factors as barriers to linguistic inclusion, such as policy–practice tensions.

title: Teacher code alternation in a Sri Lankan tertiary level EMI classroom
abstract: Abstract This study explores teacher code alternation in an English medium instruction classroom at a higher education institution in Sri Lanka. Acknowledging that code alternation is common in multilingual settings, this case study highlights its various functions, motivations, and implications for classroom purposes, addressing a gap in research within the Sri Lankan higher education context. Data were collected through classroom observations, transcriptions of recorded lessons, and semi-structured interviews. The analysis revealed five distinct functions of code alternation that aid the learning process. As a strategic linguistic tool, code alternation enhances comprehension, manages classroom dynamics, and builds rapport. Specifically, it serves to alleviate the stress of using English, foster a comfortable environment, and clarify complex ideas, thereby underscoring the importance of teacher–student perspectives on the use of code alternation for inclusive, multilingual education.

title: Where is learner agency in locally produced ELT textbooks?
abstract: Abstract This study examines how locally produced elementary-level ELT textbooks from China, Egypt, Russia, and Türkiye frame opportunities for learner participation and construct learner agency. Focusing on curricular architecture across three dimensions—multimodal and multilingual resources, localisation of contexts and content, and global citizenship and intercultural participation—we demonstrate how these textbooks structure what learners are invited to do, say, and become in classroom contexts. The findings indicate that while the materials frequently position learners as active and culturally situated participants, the forms of agency they construct are largely pedagogically managed and bounded. As a result, learner participation is often guided toward predetermined outcomes, limiting opportunities for open-ended meaning-making, critical engagement, and more expansive expressions of agency. We propose a teacher toolkit designed to support teachers in noticing opportunities for curricular modification and invite learner agency.

title: Neurodiverse perspectives on learning English in a secondary school context
abstract: Abstract This paper reports findings from a qualitative interview study conducted with nine neurodiverse students and eight of their teachers in a European secondary school context. Contrary to the results of previous studies, our teenage participants with attention deficit and hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) did not report reading difficulties in English and autistic students enjoyed peer interactions. However, both groups gave accounts of challenges with listening comprehension. Language learners with ADHD enjoyed creative, hands-on tasks but struggled with focus and emotional regulation. Autistic students excelled in structured tasks and showed attention to detail, despite often being affected by sensory sensitivities and changes in routine. Language teachers cited frequent disruptions, inconsistent academic performance, and emotional regulation difficulties among their neurodiverse students as key challenges. Several felt underprepared due to limited training in inclusive education and institutional barriers. Nevertheless, teachers highlighted the value of professional development, collaboration with parents, and fostering strong student relationships.

title: Adaptable English Language Teaching: Advances and Frameworks for Responding to New Circumstances Nima A. Nazari and A. Mehdi Riazi (eds.)
English teaching online, in politically difficult circumstances
abstract: Abstract This article explores the practices of an expert online English teacher in the politically difficult context of post-coup Myanmar. While much existing research focuses on the limitations of teaching in such settings, this study documents successful, locally adapted practice. Findings show that the teacher did not rely on advanced technologies but used low-bandwidth tools and flexible strategies to manage regular power cuts and poor internet access. Her teaching was shaped by a strong sense of care for her students, with relationship-building and emotional support seen as essential to learning. At the heart of her approach was a deep understanding of the political and social context, which informed every aspect of her technological and pedagogical decisions. These findings offer practical implications for teacher education in crisis-affected settings, arguing for a shift towards the development of strategic, context-sensitive problem-solving skills.

title: Embodied learning in microteaching: from knowing to enacting
abstract: Abstract This qualitative multiple case study investigates how microteaching supports the development of embodied pedagogical competence and teacher identity among English majors outside formal teacher education programmes in Korea. Although participants entered the course with theoretical knowledge, the first microteaching cycle revealed difficulties in task launch, interactional control, and classroom presence. Utilizing video-supported reflection and peer feedback, participants redesigned lessons in a second cycle. Findings show three shifts: participants moved from procedural replication to context-responsive adaptation; embodied strategies such as gesture and stance became more intentional; and identity evolved as learners negotiated new teacher roles. The study suggests that iterative microteaching can bridge the gap between knowing about teaching and enacting it, providing a compact practicum for English majors without school placements. Implications for designing reflective microteaching in ELT are discussed.

title: Toward affective linguistic justice in English-medium instruction
abstract: Abstract This paper examines the affective dimensions of multilingualism in English-medium instruction (EMI) in the Global South. While existing research increasingly attends to emotions in EMI, little work has theorized how affect is shaped by the ideological, historical, and political entanglements of English dominance and multilingual marginalization. The paper argues that affective experiences are central to understanding the emotional economies of EMI, showing how social imaginaries of English as a language of modernity and success generate powerful emotional attachments while simultaneously producing affective harms for multilingual learners whose linguistic repertoires are undervalued. It conceptualizes affect not as an individual reaction but as a structuring force shaped by linguistic hierarchies, neoliberal ideologies, and postcolonial histories. By foregrounding emotions as socially constructed and politically consequential, the paper proposes a framework of affective linguistic justice and outlines its implications for EMI/ELT policies and practices that seek to address linguistic inequality alongside students’ emotional lives.

title: Engaging adolescent learners in TESOL research
abstract: Abstract In the past years there have been calls in language education to engage in more inclusive research practices that also treat research subjects as co-researchers. This article focuses on a group of EFL learners who acted as researchers and developed a TESOL research project as part of their high school education. The present study describes their journey through this process, examining their initial beliefs towards research in TESOL and meaningful learning tasks, alongside their general opinions regarding this project. The findings indicated that these student researchers perceived the integration of technology into pedagogical tasks as a way to enhance EFL vocabulary learning and motivation. They considered the methodological part of the project manageable but reported difficulties in sourcing relevant literature. Overall, they were hopeful that their project would benefit other students and become an asset in their future studies.

title: Teacher Burnout from a Complex Systems Perspective Carol Griffiths (ed.)
The trap of procedural reading in ELT
abstract: Abstract In many English language teaching classrooms, learners approach reading texts primarily as sources of answers rather than as opportunities to construct meaning. This comment piece describes this pattern as procedural reading: a form of engagement shaped by repeated exposure to comprehension tasks that reward efficient answer location. While such strategies are adaptive in assessment-oriented contexts, they may narrow learners’ conception of reading and limit opportunities for deeper comprehension. Drawing on classroom observations, I explores how common task formats can influence reading behaviour and reader orientation. I then outline practical ways for teachers to rebalance task design to support both exam performance and meaningful engagement with texts. The aim is not to reject efficiency, but to restore balance between answer-focused and meaning-focused reading.

title: ELT Journal 80th Anniversary Virtual Issue
Teacher talk on social media: creating space for learning
abstract: Abstract Teachers are increasingly using social media as a form of professional development. Online teachers’ communities can be beneficial for teachers, including the opportunity to self-direct their learning, network with peers without barriers of time and space, and find support. However, we still lack an understanding of how their interactions with others help teachers learn on social media. This article reports on a study in which dialogues from a large Facebook group for English language teachers were analyzed. Different types of talk were identified in the group: talk that was productive, talk that was less productive and talk that was toxic for learning. The concept of dialogic learning frames how teachers co-construct understandings through dialogue, and what actions may enable or constrain learning. Recommendations, reflective questions and a model are provided to assist teachers and other stakeholders to understand how interactions on social media may affect opportunities for learning.

title: Differentiation in ELT: A Fresh Take on Teaching Mixed-Ability Classes Herbert Puchta and Chris Jory
Trauma and language learning: ELT classroom practices in Sri Lanka
abstract: Abstract Scholarship in the Global North has traditionally treated trauma as an individual pathological condition that needs medical intervention. However, Global South communities such as Sri Lanka approach trauma differently. Since the whole community has lived through centuries of colonization and decades of civil war, trauma is collective. For this reason, the community has developed everyday practices for a supportive environment. Such community-sponsored cultural and relational practices do not pathologize trauma. Survivors are treated as exhibiting forms of neurodiversity that come with their own strengths such as resilience, patience, and dependency. Their communication is not treated as fragmented and incoherent, but as meaningful when others co-construct meanings with them, adopting diversified semiotic resources, and going beyond normative assumptions. English language teachers have adopted pedagogical strategies influenced by such relational orientations. This article will discuss the intuitive strategies Northern Sri Lankan educators and students have adopted since the civil war.

title: Pedagogical content knowledge
Social Justice in Language Education: Taking Action, A. Biel and F. Maria Esleben (eds.)
A Casebook of Decolonizing Pedagogical Practices for Second Language Teacher Education Amy B. Gooden
Linguistic landscape for joint learning amid conflict in Israel
abstract: Abstract This article describes two ELT initiatives in Israel, offered by the English Inspectorate, aimed at learning about ‘the other’ in an area of intractable conflict. These initiatives create contact between Jews and Arabs, teachers and students, where the two school systems are separated, and contact between the communities is scarce. Both initiatives are based on linguistic landscape (LL) pedagogy that fosters activism and critical thinking. In the first initiative, teachers planned projects for learning about cultural narratives through LL. The second initiative involved collaborative work of Jewish and Arab students who met to study each other’s LL environments, inspired by the Shared Education model. The manuscript integrates visuals from the projects. We show how LL can be used to bring politically divided communities together, enabling contact in times of severe tension in long-standing conflict.

title: Compassion-based Language Education, Sarah Mercer
Reframing teachers’ role in post-conflict and crisis-affected contexts
abstract: Abstract This introduction to the special issue on teachers in post-conflict and crisis-affected contexts examines the roles, identities, and pedagogical practices of ELT professionals working in environments where instability, displacement, and violence profoundly reshape educational realities. Moving beyond policy-centred accounts, it foregrounds teachers’ lived experiences, highlighting how ELT practitioners function as multidimensional agents who combine language instruction with trauma-sensitive care, peacebuilding, and community stabilisation. The article conceptualises teacher identity and well-being as ecological and relational, shaped by systemic precarity, emotional labour, and limited institutional support. It further illustrates how context-responsive and politically charged pedagogies transform ELT classrooms into spaces of psychological safety, critical dialogue, and collective coping. The article argues for a shift away from reliance on individual teacher resilience towards coordinated professional development, policy reform, and systemic support. By centring teachers’ agency and expertise, it offers insights for stakeholders concerned with sustaining education and s

title: Effects of emotional labor on teachers in post-crisis-affected Brazil
abstract: Abstract Emotional labor plays a key role in teachers’ emotional knowledge and development. This case study focuses on how the COVID-19 pandemic has affected the lives and professional practices of a group of Brazilian English language teachers, highlighting the post-crisis emotions and emotional labor these teachers had to navigate. Data were collected through a questionnaire and narrative frames. Analysis of the data revealed that, even 5 years after the crisis, participants continue to face distress, apathy, anxiety, and fear in the classroom, stemming from the increased inequality of opportunities among learners in the challenging context of emergency remote teaching in higher education in Brazil. The study also sheds light on the implications for both pre- and in-service teachers, as well as for teacher educators, emphasizing the need to cultivate a deeper understanding of building resilience and well-being through ELT practices.

title: The demise of critical agency in a post-conflict teaching environment
abstract: Abstract In this autoethnographic study, I examine how my tension-filled lived experiences and the economic conditions of working as an English teacher in Iran have constrained my critical agency in a post-conflict teaching environment following migration. The guiding research question for this inquiry is: How is my critical agency adversely influenced and compromised in conflictual and post-conflict teaching environments? Analyses revealed that economic instability at the socio-political level, along with prescriptive teaching methods and internal deterioration, created a conflictual condition that pressured me to silence my critical agency. In the post-conflict setting of Poland, although the conditions are more supportive, the memory of past trauma and the fear of losing my current position still discourage me from openly exercising critical agency. Instead, I adopt a more conservative and innovative approach, working within existing structures to make small changes while protecting my role as a migrant academic.

title: ELT teachers and the July revolution: identity, pedagogy, and wisdom
abstract: Abstract This qualitative case study explores how ELT teachers in Bangladesh reconfigured their professional identities during the July Revolution, focusing on the nuanced role of negotiations that unfolded in classrooms amid political upheaval and emotional strain. Drawing on interviews with five university teachers and the analysis of multimodal artefacts, the study employs translanguaging pedagogy and social and emotional learning (SEL) as intersecting frameworks. The findings reveal a spectrum of teacher roles, from cautious witnesses to empathetic mentors, who responded to crisis through translanguaging practices, trauma-informed approaches, and creative multimodal strategies. This relational and ethical stance foregrounds care, presence, and cultural responsiveness as central to teaching in times of disruption. The study calls for embedding emotional literacy and context-sensitive pedagogies in teacher education to support educators in sustaining learning during periods of crisis.

title: English and the manosphere: a call for critical awareness in ELT
abstract: Abstract In recent years, the spread of online content in the form of forums, YouTube videos, podcasts, and TikTok videos has made it easier than ever for learners to access English language content to supplement their classroom learning. A disturbing part of this new online landscape is a collection of disparate communities known collectively as the manosphere. Deeply misogynist in nature, these communities view feminism as responsible for the decline of society. This manifests as a constant stream of hate-filled rhetoric against women, and the promotion of toxic masculinity. In this Comment piece, I issue a warning to language teachers of the danger that pernicious manosphere content as a site of language learning poses to language learners around the world. I also offer practical suggestions as to how teachers can use critical language pedagogy to evaluate this content in a nuanced and responsible way and help their students to construct counternarratives.

title: Advancing integrity in language assessment: Response to Bruce et al.
abstract: Abstract This Readers Respond article engages with Bruce et al. (2025), which explores UK university stakeholders’ perceptions of English language proficiency (ELP) tests. We acknowledge that such studies are motivated by the need to understand institutional contexts and priorities, while noting that more robust forms of evidence are essential for evaluations of test quality. Drawing on Plonsky’s (2024) framework for assessing research quality and transparency, we highlight opportunities to enhance future studies through the inclusion of student performance data, broader and more balanced sampling, and clear reporting of researcher affiliations. We discuss how these practices enrich interpretations of stakeholder views and support nuanced evaluations of both established and newer ELP tests. Our response aims to contribute to an ongoing, constructive dialogue about evidence-based decision-making in high-stakes assessment, emphasizing that combining multiple forms of validity evidence can help institutions make informed, fair, and transparent choices that best serve students and educational outcomes.

title: Pedagogically grounded AI use in the EFL classroom: principles and classroom examples
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is now widely available to teachers and learners through natural language prompts. While such tools create new opportunities for English language teaching, their classroom use often remains exploratory and detached from pedagogical aims. This article argues for a pedagogy-first approach, where AI use is deliberately aligned with learning objectives. Drawing on the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework and its recent adaptation to AI (AI-TPACK), the article shows how teachers can integrate technological, content, and pedagogical knowledge to ensure AI supports, rather than drives, language learning. The discussion is illustrated with adaptable and practical classroom examples that build AI literacy, enhance student engagement, and encourage critical reflection on the ethical and pedagogical boundaries of AI.

title: Navigating the English Classroom: Effective Practices for Novice Teachers
Critical questioning in language teacher education
abstract: Abstract This qualitative case study explores how the question formulation technique (QFT) facilitated critical engagement with curriculum reform among 22 Indonesian preservice EFL teachers. Conducted over 16 weeks in a private university, participants joined biweekly QFT sessions, generating 400 questions that were thematically analysed. Three key themes emerged: examining cultural norms and classroom power dynamics, addressing structural barriers, and rethinking teacher identity and agency. Findings reveal that structured questioning motivated preservice teachers to reflect on the tensions between student-centred pedagogy and local traditions. Instead of merely following curriculum mandates or copying imported teaching models, participants critically questioned hierarchical norms and considered culturally relevant adaptations. Ultimately, the QFT empowered them to move beyond passive compliance, fostering teacher agency and reflective practice. This positions preservice teachers as active interpreters of curriculum reform, capable of negotiating global pedagogical ideals with local values in EFL teacher education.

title: Reconsidering AI-detection in EFL writing: a response to De Wilde
abstract: Abstract This response engages with De Wilde’s (2024) study on novice EFL teachers’ ability to detect AI-generated writing. While endorsing her call to address AI in teacher education, I argue that her findings also expose wider pedagogical issues. First, novice teachers’ reliance on linguistic deficit cues risks pathologizing proficient learner writing, particularly in contexts where AI is permitted for language editing. Second, treating ‘personal touch’ as a marker of human authorship is increasingly unstable as large language models simulate voice convincingly. Third, drawing on recent teacher-assessment research, I contend that AI detection is a multidimensional, experience-sensitive judgement that extends beyond surface accuracy to rhetorical depth, task engagement, and teachers’ assessment beliefs; exposure to AI texts further shapes detectability. I conclude that teacher training must move from policing authorship toward developing critical AI literacy and ethically integrating AI into process-oriented writing pedagogy.

title: Looking back, moving forward: 80 volumes of ELT Journal
Teaching English and the environment to EFL young learners in Turkey
abstract: Abstract This paper reports on a part of a larger practitioner research project focused on integrating environmental issues through critical language pedagogy into a young learner’s classroom in Turkey. Drawing on Paulo Freire’s problem-posing model grounded in critical pedagogy, the authors developed localized materials, and a pedagogic model rooted in six environmental themes derived from the students’ lived experiences. The pedagogic model was implemented in a public primary setting with a group of fourth-grade students. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with the students to understand the model’s effectiveness in achieving its dual objectives: development of language and critical environmental awareness. The purpose of this paper is to present a theory-driven, practical, pedagogic model for practitioners seeking to develop their context-sensitive environmental ELT pedagogies.

title: Beyond dichotomies: unravelling the complexities of international standardised English language testing
abstract: Abstract This article discusses the issues raised in O’Sullivan’s and Hashimura et al.’s Point-Counterpoint articles with the aim of introducing new angles on the topic of international standardised English language testing and opening the debate further. In the first section, I provide summaries of the positions taken by O’Sullivan and Hashimura et al., contrasting the “tests as a social good” and “critical language testing” paradigms. Second, I explore international standardised English language testing as a site of complexity, focusing on the nature of this complexity in conceptualising language testing as a field, language tests (as social objects), and language testing organisations. Third, I address shifts towards measuring innovative constructs and the prospect of greater localisation. Finally, I conclude with a call for research that explores complexity in greater depth with a view to change.

title: Women in ELT
Pragmatics and English language education: a response to Takahashi
abstract: Abstract Readers Respond is a forum for individuals to contribute their own reactions, perspectives, or experiences in relation to a specific article or articles published in a recent issue of ELT Journal. These views are not necessarily those of the Editor, the Editorial Panel, or the Publisher. This article responds to Takahashi, S. 2025. Pragmatics in Japanese EFL Education: Textbook and Teacher Insights, ELT Journal 80/1 (this volume).

title: Principles of GenAI-assisted microlearning: perspectives of pre-service language teachers
abstract: Abstract This qualitative research explored pre-service language teachers’ perceptions of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-assisted microlearning in an ELT technology integration class. In semi-structured interviews, 14 Hong Kong pre-service teachers reflected on their engagement with adaptive, multimodal microlearning activities designed to minimize cognitive load. They valued GenAI’s personalized, real-time adaptability, interactivity, and instant feedback. However, they expressed concerns regarding learner autonomy, over-reliance on AI scaffolding, and content accuracy and transparency. They emphasized the critical role of human teachers in mediating and contextualizing GenAI use. Four pedagogical principles for effective AI-supported microlearning were identified: real-time adaptability, multimodal interactivity, learner customization, and reliability and accuracy. These principles reflect the unique affordances of the microlearning format—namely, that it is short, focused, and repeatable—rather than general GenAI features. This study provides suggestions for educators and content creators wishing to integrate GenAI thoughtfully into microlearning-based ELT.

title: International tests can benefit teachers and learners
abstract: Abstract In this paper, I present a set of arguments in support of the proposition that international standardized tests (IST) are beneficial to teachers and learners. The arguments are designed to defend the proposition from the IATEFL debate and not to offer a balanced discussion and are based on my experience as a teacher, researcher, and test developer, with some support offered from the published literature. Before presenting my arguments, I take time to briefly reflect on the drivers and objectives that lay behind the origins of standardized testing. I then consider the benefits of ISTs to learners and teachers before reflecting on the obligations of developers to teachers and learners. Without a recognition of these obligations, ISTs can never meet the needs of language learning systems.

title: Supporting student-led interactions in virtual exchange
abstract: Abstract Virtual exchange (VE) is becoming integral to many university curricula, yet students navigate VE with varying degrees of success. Despite extensive research, the role of oral interaction skills remains underexplored, especially in VE, where interactional conditions diverge from those in the classroom. This study applies conversation analysis to a fifteen-hour corpus of video-recorded meetings with students from Germany, Israel, and Spain, collaborating in online intercultural groups of three or four in an English-as-a-lingua-franca setting. Focusing on three features of the student-led interactions, namely task management, translanguaging, and cultural incidents, our findings show that conversation flow is enhanced when task management is collaborative, inclusive, and explicit, translanguaging is used strategically without excluding others, and cultural incidents are addressed constructively. These findings have important pedagogic implications for developing interactional and intercultural competence and provide essential preparation for both online and face-to-face language learners.

title: No-code approaches to developing ELT resources with generative artificial intelligence
abstract: Abstract In this series, we explore technology-related themes and topics. The series aims to discuss and demystify what may be new areas for some readers and to consider their relevance for English language teachers. Advances in the no-code approach that uses generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have enabled practitioners to develop ELT resources and tools without having programming expertise. More recently, within the ELT field, vibe coding has emerged. This approach allows instructors to develop and revise customized apps by interacting with GenAI and by using natural language alone. These innovations hold significant promise for ELT because teachers can now create resources such as chatbots for language practice, automated essay-scoring tools, and language exercise apps tailored to their needs, without relying on IT professionals. This feature article introduces three currently available approaches to developing a GenAI-mediated tool and discusses their merits and challenges in the ELT domain.

title: Genre pedagogy to teach spoken reports in EFL
abstract: Abstract Genre-based pedagogy is an approach for promoting school literacy that uses texts as basis for instruction. Since its origins in the 1980s, however, this pedagogy has emphasized written literacy, paying less attention to students’ spoken communication, particularly in EFL classrooms. To address this gap, this study assesses whether genre-based pedagogy may also promote students’ spoken communication. We adapted this pedagogy to help sixth graders create spoken descriptive reports in an EFL Colombian classroom. Our adaptation, called talking to learn (T2L), consists of a scaffolded instructional cycle that uses authentic spoken texts as the starting point for instruction. Using a case study-mixed methods design, we collected data from pre– and post–test spoken tasks, observations, and interviews. Quantitative and qualitative analyses were integrated with a joint display. Findings suggest that T2L helped students produce well-organized spoken descriptive reports, becoming a valuable tool for developing students’ ability to create meaning in EFL.

title: Making VR ordinary in ELT
Moroccan EFL teachers’ experiences with the 2023 Al-Haouz earthquake
abstract: Abstract This quantitative study examines Moroccan English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers’ experiences following the 2023 Al-Haouz earthquake, the country’s most devastating natural disaster in six decades. Using an online survey (n = 133) grounded in social-emotional learning (SEL), trauma-sensitive pedagogy, and resilience frameworks, the study explored teachers’ experiences in relation to challenges, growth, coping mechanisms, and preparedness levels. Descriptive analyses revealed significant emotional and professional strain, including material loss, disrupted instruction, and limited institutional support. Yet, most teachers reported sustained commitment to teaching and strong reliance on personal and relational coping resources such as faith, community support, and helping others. Findings highlight teachers’ dual roles as educators and emotional caregivers and underscore the urgency of integrating trauma-sensitive practices and SEL principles into national teacher preparation and crisis recovery plans. The study contributes to growing discussions on teacher well-being, autonomy, and resilience in disaster-affected educational contexts.

title: Fairness for sale: the hidden costs of international language tests
abstract: Abstract This Counterpoint challenges the claim that international standardised assessments benefit both learners and teachers. While acknowledging that such tests are unlikely to disappear, we argue that they harm language education. We first deconstruct the historical myths used to legitimise standardisation, revealing it as a rhetorical move that substitutes genealogy for evidence. We then trace the resulting harms in three ways: mechanistically, through overstandardisation that flattens language and threatens validity; systemically, through the economic machinery of the testing-industrial complex, where ‘edu-washing’ casts profit as benevolence; and ideologically, through a fiction of fairness that conflates sameness with justice, concealing raciolinguistic, and algorithmic biases. Against this, we propose a human-centred re-orientation of assessment, where validity is both statistical and ethical, and fairness an ongoing relationship rather than a calculation. Reform, we suggest, will not come from better metrics but from empathy, from a willingness to remember what it feels like to be measured.

title: Beyond detection: GenAI in EAL writing education
abstract: Abstract This study investigates how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) shapes the writing practices of five Chinese English as an additional language (EAL) students and how emerging GenAI-text detection practices mediate that use. Findings from screen-recordings, written drafts, and interviews reveal four recurrent functions of GenAI use, that is, brainstorming, structuring, occasional drafting, and revising, yet students calibrated their reliance on each function against the perceived risk of being flagged by GenAI detectors. To mitigate that risk, participants shuttled between ChatGPT, Grammarly, and self-paraphrase to ‘humanise’ GenAI output, occasionally reallocating effort from idea development to surface revision. The study, therefore, problematises a detection-first approach, showing that it (1) engenders strategic but pedagogically hollow text manipulation, (2) complicates ‘plagiarised’ versus ‘original’ writing, and (3) potentially shifts assessment towards product-centric criteria. The study argues for cultivating critical AI literacy so that GenAI-assisted EAL writing instruction can prioritize creativity, voice, and argument quality over algorithmic policing.

title: Reimagining ELT: nomadic knowledging and nomadic languaging
abstract: Abstract Drawing on an ethnographic study with the Mongolian nomadic herders - xууч xөөрөх - loosely translated as “nomadic reminiscing circle,” this article seeks to expand the growing decolonial languaging turn in ELT. It introduces the intertwined land-based cosmologies of “nomadic knowledging” and “nomadic languaging,” drawing on a philosophy where life, nature, time, language, and identity are understood as inherently fluid but attuned to the cycles of the land. Yet, this fluidity exists in tension with the contextual rootedness - the need for linguistic boundaries to protect nomadic knowledge systems. English is welcomed into the Mongolian nomadic cosmologies only when it enters with humility, respect and care. This tension highlights that the languaging turn in ELT must attend not only to fluidity but also to rootedness. Just as nomads adapt to ever-changing environments, ELT must remain responsive to shifting identities, evolving language practices and contextualized local practices.

title: Pragmatics in Japanese EFL education: textbook and teacher insights
abstract: Abstract This study examined how the most recent government-approved English textbooks and high school English teachers in Japan address pragmatics in the context of speech acts. A page-by-page analysis of twelve textbooks coded explicitly presented general pragmatic information, along with the types and presentation formats of speech acts. Teachers’ awareness and instruction of pragmatic content were explored through an online survey of forty-six in-service high school teachers and follow-up interviews with a subset of five participants. The textbook analysis revealed limited coverage of pragmatics and little information on the contextual use of speech acts. The teacher survey suggested that although many teachers had limited knowledge of pragmatics, they compensated for textbook limitations in improvised ways rather than through systematic planning. The study concludes that while textbook designers and teachers should address pragmatics in a consistent and sufficient manner, the absence of a standardized curriculum of pragmatics may hinder this goal.

title: Using ChatGPT as a “Friend” in reflective critical friendships
abstract: Abstract Reflective practice has long been regarded as a cornerstone of language teacher education and development, typically enacted through dialogue with trusted colleagues or critical friendships (CFs). Such human-to-human exchanges are grounded in trust, contextual understanding, and professional experience, and they play a central role in shaping teachers’ professional development. The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT, however, invites new possibilities for reflection by offering teachers instant access to dialogue that is probing, structured, and nonjudgmental. This study examines the potential of ChatGPT to act as a form of CF in reflective practice, comparing its contributions with those of human interlocutors. We consider benefits such as immediacy, breadth of perspectives, and creative provocation, alongside significant limitations, including the absence of trust, lived experience, and relational aspects. Ethical concerns, particularly those relating to bias, cultural representation, privacy, and the risk of over-reliance, are also foregrounded. We argue that while ChatGPT may usefully supplement reflective practice, especially fo

title: Early Foreign Language Learning and Teaching. Evidence Versus Wishful Thinking
Facilitating professional growth through materials-based assessments
abstract: Abstract The burgeoning scholarship about teaching materials has been reflected in a growing number of teacher education courses including instruction in materials development. However, we know little about how student–teachers in teacher education courses develop a knowledge base about materials which they can use in their practice as English language teacher. Addressing the dearth of publications in materials development in teacher education, here we report findings from a study that explored the impact of a professional development qualification for in-service teachers that uses materials evaluation, adaptation, and creation as the core components of assessment. Data from multiple interviews with three teacher participants shows that the articulation of materials evaluation, adaptation, and design in the assessed tasks granted them concrete opportunities to develop in the areas of materials adaptation and design. This allows teachers to meet learners’ needs as well as developing their professional confidence.

title: Trauma-sensitive English teaching and SEL amid war in Ukraine
abstract: Abstract The 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine unleashed a collective trauma that has impacted all within the country, including educators attempting to support their students. This action research explored how an English teacher in Ukraine implemented and evaluated classroom activities founded upon trauma-sensitive teaching, social-emotional learning, and resilience-building. Participants completed individual activity surveys and a final survey. In response to the research question: How do students living and learning in a wartime crisis perceive teaching strategies based in trauma-sensitive teaching, social-emotional learning, and resilience building in the English classroom?, descriptive statistics determined that students rated all activities positively. Qualitative analysis of participant comments found that students: described the activities as engaging and distracting them from their worries; valued the discussions for both connection-building and language development; felt the limits of their English proficiency; and demonstrated the complex responses of those living through ongoing war-related trauma.

title: Teaching English in Iran in the shadow of sanctions
Children’s learning through digital technologies: an introduction
abstract: Abstract This introductory article sets the scene for this Special Issue on ‘Children’s Learning Through Digital Technologies’. We begin by outlining key issues in this area: the valuable opportunities such technologies offer children to develop English language and other skills; their limited use in primary English classrooms; the relative scarcity of research into 6- to 14-year-olds’ digital activity which generally focuses on just a few research settings. We then introduce the seven Special Issue contributions that explore children’s digital experiences at home and school, teachers’ perceptions, classroom practices, and teaching strategies. The articles also showcase age-appropriate methods for working with children. Finally, we consider some broader implications and challenges of integrating digital technologies into children’s learning. Our aim is for this Special Issue to encourage practitioners and researchers to consider how digital technologies can be used and studied in their own young learner contexts.

title: Enjoyment, engagement, and success in children’s digital EFL games
abstract: Abstract Game-based language learning can be enjoyable and effective for young learners, but it is not clear that enjoyment precipitates effectiveness. We investigated the relationships between engagement and success in game-based language learning for young language learners. This study reports data from 125 Spanish/Catalan 11- to 12-year-old students playing EFL literacy minigames. Learners answered a questionnaire about engagement with English classes and with the minigames, and gameplay data were collected from the game logs. We show that increased minigame use was due to successful language use during gameplay or positive attitudes towards the use of game-based language learning, but not both for the same students. Clustering students based on engagement revealed that an otherwise-unengaged group became engaged with language content through game use. We encourage the use of game-based language learning for children as one activity among many, including the use of supplementary materials to help learners understand that games can be effective language-learning tools.

title: Digital game-based language learning in the young L2 learner classroom
abstract: Abstract Digital game-based language learning (DGBLL) aims to enhance L2 learners’ language and literacy skills through the purposeful integration of digital games not designed for language practice. This approach can provide opportunities for learners to be exposed to and use L2 in authentic, meaningful contexts, with a focus on both meaning and form. It can also promote collaboration, creative problem solving, and critical thinking, and is associated with situated learning, intrinsic motivation, and clear objectives and assessment. This article sets out some practical considerations to guide practitioners in planning for and designing DGBLL. It then analyses three DGBLL exemplars, designed and implemented by the author in young L2 learner classrooms in Spain and Hong Kong. Each exemplar is evaluated using a framework based on the principles of task-based language teaching and ideas drawn from the broader literature on game-based learning.

title: Exploring six-year-olds’ L2 English digital learning in the home
abstract: Abstract Young L2 English learners constitute an underresearched group in the fields of L2 acquisition and ELT. However, emerging research has shown that young children learn English informally, even prior to formal instruction in school, often influenced by their engagement in English-language media, such as watching YouTube and gaming. This study adopts an ethnographic perspective to explore how three six-year-olds in Norway engage with English-language media platforms and games in their homes, and how such engagement influences L2 learning. The study’s focus is on methodological and ethical issues when researching children in private spheres. Data were collected through a show-and-tell procedure which demanded thorough ethnographic groundwork and considerable researcher flexibility. The findings showed that all three homes offered affordances for L2 learning. We argue that in order to capture socially situated engagement with digital technologies, it was crucial to collect data in the actual socially situated practice in the young learners’ homes.

title: Agency
Primary EFL teachers’ perceptions of technology to support speaking
abstract: Abstract This study examines the perceptions of pre-service and in-service teachers on the use of technology-enhanced tasks to support children in speaking English in diverse primary EFL classrooms. Research on both primary EFL teachers’ perceptions and technology-enhanced speaking tasks for young learners is scant. This study addresses these gaps by exploring the views of participating pre-service and in-service EFL teachers. To gather data, three technology-enhanced projects were implemented in primary EFL classrooms and participant interviews conducted. Prior to data collection, a workshop was held to train participants in using technology. Interview findings suggest that participants considered various aspects of gamification, such as sequencing tasks, competition, and collaboration, to be crucial when designing and implementing technology-enhanced tasks to support young foreign language learners in speaking English. The results also highlight teachers’ desire for greater support, including teacher training, to enable them to implement such tasks.
